item.text:
{"answers":[{"question_id":"Q026_protein_kinase_like_function_transfer","answer":"Canonical protein kinases, aminoglycoside phosphotransferases (APHs), and phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks) share the protein kinase-like catalytic architecture, associated with SCOPe fold d.144 and superfamily d.144.1 in the α+β class. Superfamily membership supports remote common ancestry of the catalytic core; fold similarity alone establishes structural resemblance, and class membership is much broader. These relationships do not make the three groups one substrate-specific family.

Their related, typically two-lobed cores position a nucleotide donor and an acceptor for phosphoryl transfer, commonly using ATP and divalent metal ions. This supports a shared catalytic framework, not identical catalytic details or guaranteed activity in every member. Canonical protein kinases generally phosphorylate protein Ser, Thr, or Tyr residues; APHs phosphorylate hydroxyl groups on aminoglycosides; PI3Ks phosphorylate the 3-hydroxyl of the inositol headgroup of phosphoinositide lipids. Protein-substrate preferences, antibiotic resistance profiles, and lipid-substrate preferences cannot be transferred across these groups from architecture alone.

Specificity transfer requires family/subfamily placement and phylogenetic evidence, sequence and structural conservation of catalytic and substrate-contacting residues, and preferably substrate-bound structures. Canonical protein-kinase motifs must be assessed in context rather than required unchanged in divergent kinases. Direct biochemical evidence should establish activity, substrate range, kinetics, and product identity or phosphorylation position; structural membership alone cannot exclude an inactive kinase-like protein.

Regulatory transfer additionally requires evidence for the relevant regulatory domains, phosphorylation sites, interacting subunits, localization, and cellular context, supported by binding and functional perturbation experiments. Activation-loop control in a protein kinase, for example, does not establish equivalent control in an APH or PI3K; PI3K regulatory mechanisms also differ among classes. A distant member can provide a template for the conserved catalytic core, but substrate-binding loops, regulatory interfaces, and conformational states need closer templates or independent validation.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
